sections.title: Activity: pick your passive safety environment
Activity: alter your passive safety environment

blocks.p: The main aim of Environmental Anchors is to increase the number and effectiveness of passive safety cues that your nervous system detects from your surroundings. The environment is the best place to start since you have control over it and can deliberately set up continuous passive safety cues. With time, these cues can become strong safety anchors as you mindfully and intentionally experience them.

In this section, I'll discuss different aspects of your environment that you can consider changing or adjusting. Your task is determining which changes work best for you by paying attention to how you feel in response to these options.

By intentionally creating a supportive and calming external space, you offer your nervous system a backdrop of safety, which can positively impact your overall well-being and resilience. The ultimate goal is to build an environment with enough consistent passive safety cues to activate your safety state. Think of this as a passive safety cue platform from which you will continue to build even more safety.

Building safety doesn't involve deep meditative practices. However, it does include lots of mindfulness. So, you will be looking inward and noticing how you feel. Looking inward is not necessarily easy, and neither are extended moments of mindfulness through meditation. Something that can make small or extended mindfulness moments more achievable is an environment that cues safety within your system. Adjusting your environment now will pay dividends for you in the future. It will make your other safety practices easier.

Dr. Porges said, "once the passive pathway effectively shifts our physiological state, the second step can be initiated." We must set passive cues before moving on to the more active ones. The environment is a great place to start implementing passive safety cues.

Your environment can influence the activity of your ventral vagal pathways. Surroundings cause you to feel more or less safety, directly affecting your SSIEC domains, like cognitions and emotions. Right now, enough safety cues surround you to access and maintain a mixed state of stillness. There is nothing you need to do or change to remain in stillness. You passively neurocept the safety cues from your current environment, allowing you to immobilize and read this.

However, you could take things to the next level and mindfully experience the passive safety cues from the environment. You would intentionally notice the pieces of the environment and which feel safer than not. Rather than simply passively neurocepting them as safety, you consciously notice how they impact your state and overall experience of the present moment.

For example, opening your blinds to let in natural sunlight may provide a passive safety cue. That neuroception may shift your state into more safety than when the blinds are closed. You can exist within this space with the passive neuroception of safety and focus on other things, like work. But you can intentionally enhance the safety neuroception and potentially anchor by pausing work, then mindfully experiencing the light filling the room, focusing on shadows, highlights, and colors. This mindfulness further connects you to the experience of the present moment through your senses and then your awareness of the general level of safety within you.

On the other hand, some environments may trigger your defensive pathways. Crowded streets or busy places like the Department of Motor Vehicles (especially without an appointment) can be neurocepted as dangerous due to proximity to others, harsh lighting, and loud sounds. These types of sensory inputs push you away from your safety state. Perhaps not so much to get you mobile enough to run away or fight, but far enough from safety to lose your anchoring and notice a shift within. If you exist in a chronic defensive state, these inputs solidify it, making it even more difficult to access your safety state.
While there are general examples of passive safety and danger cues, we each have individual experiences. A cue of safety for me could be a cue of danger for you.

Let's look at the example of a cemetery to illustrate the various possible safety and danger cues. A cemetery might generally be considered a cue of danger due to the nature of death and grief. But it may also be a safety cue due to the environmental greenery, landscaping, and general quiet. If you have a loved one who has passed and is in the cemetery, you may feel a sense of connection. But that feeling of connection can also bring a deep feeling of sadness. Maybe even anger at your loss. You might even have defensive feelings when you notice the flowers at their site are missing or wilted. Point being, one environment can have numerous potential subjective safety and danger cues.

On top of general cues, environments can act as potent triggers for memories of past traumatic incidents. These triggers vary significantly among individuals, as specific contextual cues may provoke defensive feelings in one person but not others. My former podcast host, Mercedes Corona (LMFT), shared with me about a therapy client triggered by the chess board in her therapy office. That chess board connects to memories of traumatic incidents in that person's life. That same chessboard could be a safety cue for another client who associates it with quality time with their parent during childhood.

So, while we're discussing the environment as a whole, our focus is more on its specific components, particularly those within your control. These minor elements contribute to the overall neuroception of environmental safety and danger. It's not just the DMV or the cemetery, but specific aspects like the uncomfortable plastic chairs or the green lawn. These particular elements contribute to the neuroceptions of safety and danger.

You probably have very little control over the majority of environments in your daily life. Maybe you can change things at your desk at work (if you have one). But when you go to the DMV, or a library, or a meeting at work, or visit someone's home, you don't get to alter the environment to suit your neuroceptions of safety. But you have a home and this is the perfect place to start.

Ideally, your entire home is a cue of safety for you. But realistically, it's not. Your kids, spouse, or roommate might be too loud or leave their stuff lying around. Or maybe you're the one leaving clutter around the home and putting off cleaning for another time. (You'll totally get to it, I believe you!) You can apply this lesson to your entire home if you like. But that might be overwhelming. Instead, let's focus on one spot and work outward as you're ready.

blocks.h3: Activity: pick your passive safety environment

blocks.p: Your task right now is to identify one spot in your home that will serve as your "Passive Safety Environment." You have two options for identifying one:

ul: Pick the spot you want to be the safest in your home, but it is not currently.
Pick the spot that is currently the safest and can be enhanced.

blocks.p: Your safety environment is a space that you will return to again and again. Creating this environment might be the most immediately impactful change you can make at this stage of your journey. To find your safety environment, follow these steps:

ol: Spend a few moments in every space in your home.
Notice what levels of safety each space brings you: name the feelings, rate each room from 0 to 5 (5 being the safest), or ask yourself if you genuinely want to spend more time in this space.
Notice or journal about how this space brings you to your safety state (or not).

blocks.p: Congrats! You've identified a space in your home. This environment is where you will focus your efforts in this lesson. We'll call this your "Passive Safety Environment." This little space will provide you with constant passive safety cues while you're in it. You can use this passive safety platform to mindfully experience the other safety cues and anchors. Later, it can be the foundation for directly experiencing your stuck defensive state.

The sensory aspects of your surroundings are imperative in neurocepting safety. [Sensory safety anchors](piece:sensory-anchors) go further, but for now, let's concentrate on the overall ambiance of your Passive Safety Environment. When creating passive safety cues in your surroundings, I encourage you to consider these elements, control them, and refine them to enhance your space's overall sense of safety.

We're not all interior designers, and that's okay. Simple actions like rearranging or discarding items can make a difference. There may be an object in one room that could enhance the safety of another space. You could swap it out or add it to your designated safety environment. It could be as simple as moving a rug, a blanket, or a cherished memento to create a more comforting space.

If you have the time and the money to invest in a space, great. However, I don't expect you to incur debt or spend any money at all to get more safety in your identified environment. You don't need to paint walls or buy furniture. There are probably small, free things you can do to enhance safety, starting now. Let's delve into the specific elements of your environment.

Colors will trigger a sense of safety or danger in you, although it might not provoke an obvious response. Imagine entering a room where everything is orange: orange walls, furniture, keyboard, screens, and so on. Take a moment to imagine how you would feel in that space. Does it feel more calming and peaceful, or does it make you more nauseous?

Now, picture walking into a room of blues, greens, and perhaps some browns or neutral tones. These colors are typically a reliable safety cue. If you're similar to me, you might feel a sense of lightness and welcome when surrounded by those colors. Essentially, your safety system becomes activated. (I assume that common colors of nature are a predictable safety cue.)

Does this mean you should ban any oranges from your space and live only with natural blues and greens? Of course not. We're talking about the extremes to make a point. Realistically, we want a balance of colors that help you feel settled. You're probably not an interior designer. Don't worry about creating a whole new look for your home. For now, just notice what colors you're drawn to. Then, start implementing them into your identified safety space.
Take a moment to look around and observe your surroundings.

ul: Notice the colors present and determine which one stands out the most.
Do you have any positive or negative feelings toward this color?
Note the colors in your environment that provide you with more safety than less.

blocks.p: Painting all your walls might be unrealistic. However, I'm sure you can introduce pleasing colors into your little Passive Safety Environment. Consider swapping out objects in your space that bring in the color you feel a safety cue from. Perhaps there's a vase in another room that you could bring into your designated safety space. Or there's something from the outdoors that you could bring in. My son and I enjoy cutting roses from our backyard and bringing them indoors. Their vibrancy adds a sense of beauty and playfulness to our space. These small, manageable changes can make a significant difference in creating a space that cues safety.

Think about how you feel when you enter a room crammed with furniture or recall navigating through a classroom filled with desks and backpacks as a child. Did these situations feel comfortable or uncomfortable? Did they evoke a sense of liking or disliking?

They may result in a general feeling of irritability or tension. This isn't a big deal if it's just once. But if you're constantly navigating tight spaces, the irritation could accumulate. Creating a space with better proximity for comfort can help your system breathe easier and give you more time in your ventral vagal safety state.

I'm a tall drink of water at six feet tall. Spaciousness is a big issue for me. Our previous house was more cramped, and I often felt irritable as I often unsuccessfully navigated through the stuff in the house and the people and pets within it. I'd stumble over things and bang my hips into the kitchen counter. Our current home is larger, providing more space and ease to my system. (Though the kitchen and laundry room are still a challenge.)

When altering your Passive Safety Environment's spaciousness, consider what is best for your daily life. But also keep in mind what is best for practicing safety. You'll use this space for practicing the other anchors, including [body movements](piece:anchor-movement-body-breath). If you can, leave a pocket of space to allow for movement you already enjoy, like yoga or dance. If this is not possible, don't worry; there are many options for movement.
Take a moment to notice the proximity of the space around you.

ul: Notice any general feelings of liking or disliking.
How much space do you have, and how do you feel about it?
Is there something you can move to create more physical spaciousness? Or something to move to create a tighter, cozier feel?

blocks.p: We've been discussing physical space, but visual space is important too. I appreciate minimal, clean lines and a balance between not too much and not too little. You may have a different experience. But in general, a less visually cluttered space is less overwhelming. Walking into a simplified room might evoke a sense of expansiveness and relaxation.

However, a space filled with items can also be appealing, provided it's tidy and organized. Imagine a grand library filled with rows and rows of books. Or a wall of books in those homes that are good enough for a magazine spread. It's just stuff and lots of it. Dust collectors, really.

But visually, they look fantastic. Why? Because they're tidy and organized. The amount of stuff in a space is not necessarily a danger cue. If those books in that library or magazine home were stacked on top of each other or strewn about the floor, you would not get the same sense of calm and peace.
Look around you and notice the level of tidiness or lack thereof.

ul: Check in with feelings of like or dislike.
Can you identify something you can change right now?

blocks.p: Darkness is typically a danger cue. Even a poorly lit corner of a room can be enough to trigger a slight sense of danger. Or a dark hallway. Conversely, too much light can also be a danger cue. These potential danger cues interrupt or cut off one of our senses: sight. In response, our system shifts away from safety and toward danger.

Clients often report feeling more restless at night: anxiety, panic, and fear increase. They can only embrace the darkness, settle into stillness, and finally sleep when their safety state is active. However, settling is more challenging if darkness is a significant danger cue for them. Darkness can also enhance their other potential danger cues, like being alone or in silence. Maybe you can relate.

Is there a correct amount of light that you should surround yourself with? No. It comes down to yourself as an individual, of course. But more specifically, it comes down to what state you're in from moment to moment. When in a state of safety, the lighting you tolerate differs from when in flight/fight and shutdown.

In shutdown, you probably do better with dim lighting or even darkness. As you emerge from shutdown, you're probably more capable of being in environments with more light. And in safety, you will probably not only be okay with light but also crave sunlight. In safety, you can also embrace darkness and settle into stillness for sleep or dance with another in play under the dim bulbs at a wedding. (I'll be alone at my table. I'm fine, but thanks for your concern.) You may experience the flashing lights of a concert or fireworks with pleasure and excitement from your playful, sympathetic state. (I'll wait in the car. Again, I'm fine, I promise.)

However, there are probably general types of lighting that cause a slight cue of danger to our system. Lights that are bright white, like fluorescent ones, are probably typically less calming than natural light or warmer lights. And if a light is flickering or humming, that is probably less safety-activating than one constantly on and quiet.
Take a moment now to notice the lighting in your immediate space.

ul: How does it make you feel? Do you like or dislike it?
Is there something you can change in your immediate space's lighting?

blocks.p: Artificial and natural sounds surround us: cars, air conditioners, wind, people, birds, etc. But some sounds provide more cues of safety than others. And the lack of sound can also be a cue of safety or danger.

You may be unaware, but right now, you're likely surrounded by a constant hum of various machines, like computers, refrigerators, and overhead lights. Even outside, there are sounds like lawn mowers and distant traffic. There's likely a continual low-level auditory assault that you're constantly processing. Those sounds fade into the background, out of your conscious awareness, but they still affect your state. (If you don't hear these things, where are you and can I join you? I'll be quiet, I promise.)

Our evolutionary ancestors didn't have to deal with this constant stream of noise. At least, not streams of noise that we have. They lived in relative silence, punctuated by the sounds of nature. We've lost our connection with silence. It must have once been a friend to those who came well before us. When the silence or normal rhythm of nature was interrupted, it indicated there may be danger.

For us, silence can be settling or unsettling. Again, this depends on the person, and especially on their state. In flight/fight, we may do well with noise. Actually, we may create our own noise, raising our voices to impose our will upon others. In shutdown, noise is best at a minimum. In safety, we can embrace a loud concert but still smile with a friend or close our eyes in silence.

Generally, less noise is better: less volume, less echoes, less sound distortions. Natural noises are generally better than artificial noises. A breeze through the trees is probably more of a safety cue than the hum of a refrigerator. The sound of actual instruments is probably more appealing than digital (especially when they have unintended digital distortions).

As you create your safety environment, consider reducing the intensity of noise. It's noticeably different when you enter a room that's been adequately sound-dampened. It's quieter, calmer, and feels better. You can add or rearrange soft items in your environment that absorb sound and reduce echo: furnishings, carpets, rugs, and blankets. While having blankets hanging everywhere might not be visually appealing, you could set up a temporary space for a meditation session to experience reduced sound.

If you have the money for it, look into sound panels. My home office has two sound panels on each wall (2 by 4 feet), which dampens echo. (If you watch me on YouTube, it's the blue rectangle behind me on my podcast.) The panels make a substantial difference compared to the rest of the house. When I walk into the office, there is a noticeable sound dampening, which significantly settles my system. These are a financial investment in the hundreds, but they make a big difference. However, pillows, blankets, and other soft things can have the same effect. (A walk-in closet is great for this, too.)

Another option is to turn off whatever mild sound-producing things you can that are around you. It may be things you left on or could be more obvious: the exhaust hood over your stove, bathroom fans, lights, and TVs. Stop and listen to what is around you and what you have control over. Likewise, if the silence is distressing, think about adding soothing sounds, white noise, or music.
Take a moment to notice the sound of your immediate space.

ul: Is there silence or a constant hum?
Do you notice feelings of like or dislike for the individual sound pieces?
Can you notice sounds that are closer or farther away?
What sounds can you control right now?

blocks.p: You have lots of potentially safety-enhancing environmental pieces to consider already. But what about your position in the environment? More specifically, what position will you likely spend the most time in within your Passive Safety Environment? And what cues of safety does that positioning allow for?

Your position refers to the direction you face and your body's posture in that space. When altering your Passive Safety Environment, experiment with where your chair(s) face and how it feels. Does it feel safer for you to face a window or a wall? Do you prefer to be in the middle of the room or a corner?

On top of the direction you face, comfort level is also a factor to consider. Add or swap out seating that allows for more comfort. If you have the funds, buy the perfect seating for your safety wants and needs. If not, swap a piece of furniture out for one from another room. Or, remove seating altogether and set up a comfy spot on the floor with blankets and pillows.
(Don't hurt yourself with these alterations, by the way. Meaning don't pull, strain, or tweak any muscles. Ask for help from someone, or just focus on what you can control.)

In my home office, I spend the most time in a corner chair when I do my meditative and safety anchoring practices. The chair faces the windows of the office with a view of the greenery of the front yard. (Although, the corner can feel too cramped at times. Oh, and the dang neighbors keep parking their cars in front of my house and it drives me up the wall.) In the mornings, I like to sip my coffee with a view of the backyard. And in the evenings, I feel the most grounded on a chair on the deck in the backyard.
Take a moment to notice your positioning within your immediate space.

ul: What are you facing? What are you able to see? What are you unable to see?
Do you have a general feeling of liking or disliking your current positioning?
What is your posture?
Do you have a general feeling of liking or disliking your current posture?

blocks.h3: Activity: alter your passive safety environment

blocks.p: You've mindfully experienced the individual environment pieces in your immediate space. And you've made some notes about what is activating safety or not. Great job. Now, take all these individual pieces of the environment and focus on your Passive Safety Environment. Within it, start to add, remove, or alter these pieces one at a time:

ul: color
spaciousness
tidiness
lighting
sound
positioning

blocks.p: As you adjust, check in with yourself and see if it does indeed cause you to feel more safety than less. If so, keep the adjustment and move on to the next environmental piece.

Make minor tweaks to your Passive Safety Environment as often as you need. Don't repaint your environment week in and week out. But you can make minor alterations, like items on a shelf or chair positioning, as you see fit. I also recommend keeping the space clean and tidy: so no wrappers, crumbs, or socks lying around!

Your environmental safety cues might change as you gain more safety in your system. A chair in the corner (facing away from it) will work well for flight/fight activation but less so for safety and a need for expansiveness. Dim lighting in shutdown is great, but you may need to enhance your lighting as sympathetic energy flavors your system. Be curious, be open, and change what you need to when needed.

blocks.why: Your space is set up. This practice anchors you in it, through what you see.

ol: The environment provides passive neuroceptions of safety and danger. You can control the amount and quality of passive safety cues within your environment.
You can turn passive safety cues into mindful safety anchors.
You can change your environment to suit your system's needs as you anchor more deeply into safety.

blocks.prompt: Did this provide you with any new experiences of safety?
Was this challenging for you? What about it was challenging?
Is this something you can continue to practice?
What three pieces of the environment did you find the most beneficial? Do they have anything in common?
